I think there is more to this than that. 

I see this being called in the current tests, and even though the tests are ignored here, the tests for which it is called are actually still later executed correctly.  That was what had me really confused.

Every test is treated as if it had an invisible CombinatorialAttribute,
just in case any values are found. That's probably the call you are seeing.
If it's a generic method that doesn't have data attributes on the
arguments, then nothing is found, so no cases are generated.

However, I have succeeded in creating true generic tests like my examples.
Some of them work and some don't. Some an never work, unless we change the
meaning of Combinatorial.

As you see from the milestone assigned, I don't actually plan on working
this any time soon though.

> From: CharliePoole [mailto:notifications@github.com]
> Sent: Saturday, November 22, 2014 6:55 AM
> To: nunit/nunit
> Subject: [nunit] CombiningStrategyAttributes don't work correctly on
> Generic methods (#377)
> 
> This test works OK...
> 
> [Test, Combinatorial]
> public void MyTest(
> [Values(1, 2)] T x
> [Values(3, 4)] T y)
> {
> }
> 
> It generates four test cases: (1,3) (1,4) (2,3) (2,4) and all of them
> match the signature of the method with T == int.
> 
> But this doesn't...
> 
> [Test, Combinatorial]
> public void MyTest(
> [Values(1, "2")] T x
> [Values(3, "4")] T y)
> {
> }
> 
> It generates four test cases: (1,3) (1,"4") ("2",3) ("2","4") where only
> two of them match the signature of the method, the first with T == int and
> the fourth where T == string.
> 
> Similar behavior will occur for Pairwise and Sequential attributes.
> 
> Making this work in all cases will be very complicated. Currently the CF
> build simply ignores any combining attribute when the method is generic.
> Really, it should give an error.
> 
> We may want to deal with this in stages.
> 1. Give an error message when one of these attributes is used on a generic
>    method.
> 2. Pick out the easy-to-implement cases and accept them. For example,
>    methods of one argument.
> 3. Do a final fix that handles all cases.
> 
> Since nobody seems to have ever noticed this over the years, I'm keeping
> it at a normal priority even though it's a bit of a shock!
>

Since we now have Sergey to work on this, I'm moving it to Alpha 4.

Here's my current (non-definitive) take on the issue.

The example that fails is an error on the part of the user. Some other errors, like mixing int and double, might not be errors since we can perform a conversion from int to double. We have to be careful to detect only real errors.

We can either give a general error on the method itself: Sorry, because of the arguments you specified, some test cases would be invalid, so we are giving up. Or we can be specific, generate all the cases and mark the ones that are incorrect as not runnable. I prefer the second approach, for two reasons:
1. It gives the user better info. The mismatched cases would display and the user could see exactly why the chosen values don't work in this context.
2. It leverages existing code that generates cases, whereas the first approach would involve an extremely complicated analysis that parallels what we already do without using the code.

Some experimentation is needed to figure out what the compiler does for generic methods versus what .NET does. My guess is that there is code to make sure that both arguments of a method call like the one given are specialized to the same type. .NET seems very happy to allow us to specialize 
SomeMethod<T>(T x, T y) to SomeMethod(int x, string y) and that's what we are doing!
The CF generic issues could be relevant here.  Although, if the interface to the Datapoint Providers is modified to allow for probing, it should be possible to do what I have done elsewhere.

I think that making CF work like the other builds with respect to generic
methods is a further step we will need to take. The error we are dealing
with here applies to all builds.

I would like to understand how we are getting Combinatorial and Pairwise to
work at all on CF, given the conditional code that seems to skip processing
for generic methods. Have you debugged through a loading of a generic test
method with one of those attributes applied? Is the method already
specialized to (object, object) when you get to that point?

Looks very similar to what I did in MakeGenericMethodEx, although in a different context.

I hadn't thought of that, but of course that's a bad Test Case. I would have thought we gave a proper NotRunnable result for it, but apparently not. I wonder if this has been a problem all along, even in NUnit 2.x. Anyway, what you are doing looks reasonable and but will be tons easier to review as a pull request .

As a point of process, you should do a  PR when you are ready to merge OR when you have code that you want looked over. Just say what you want done at the top of the PR. PRs basically give us a specialized discussion forum about the work you are doing - just like the issue does - plus the ability for us to pull down the code and run it and to make line-by-line comments on the code.

Hmm, NUnit 2 has a different behavior.

`TestCase( 1, "2" )` works for NUnit 2, but doesn't work for NUnit 3.

And `TestCase( 1, "Two" )` doesn't work for both NUnit 2 and NUnit 3.

So it looks like to keep backward compatibility with NUnit 2 we also need to check if argument can be converted to the target type. I'll check NUnit 2 source code.

Also, I’m wondering if it’s worth trying to combine this fix and MakeGenericMethodEx...

I will create a pull request for the updated fix.

It would be nice to have a single method that was used everywhere, and that worked for all platforms.  I use MakeGenericEx in a number of places already.  However, when you have the ability to work with open generic definitions (all non-CF platforms) the code can be a lot simpler, and a lot more deterministic.

The conversion is unintended and 3.0 isn't required to be 100% compatible
with 2.0. In fact, I'd call the 2.x behavior a bug, since we are only
supposed to do the same conversions that the compiler would do without a
cast.

However, I do recall that we had something special in TestCase, which was
intended to deal with the fact that you can't have an attribute argument
that's a decimal.

You should be aware that TestCase has extra conversions from all the other
data attributes, intended to deal with the issue of limited types for use
as attribute arguments. It probably makes sense to get other attributes
working first.

A suggestion: don't try to make the issue be "everything that's wrong with
generics." Fix one thing and get it in the build, then find something else
to fix. That said, there's nothing wrong with scoping out the problem.

Charlie
